2. The plaintiff's case is that the disputed land belonged to defendant No. 1 in raiyati right and he con traced to sell the land to the plaintiff for a sum of Rs. 4,250/- out of which Rs. 2,000/- was paid on 15-11-56 by way of earnest money. In token of the said contract there was a deed of agreement for sale, according to which the sale deed was to be executed after obtaining Income Tax Clearing Certificate and payment of the balance of the consideration. Although the plaintiff was put into possession of the disputed land in pursuance of the said contract, defendant No 1 subsequently changed his mind and executed a patta and a kabala in favour of defendant Nos. 2 and 3. Defendant No. 1 having failed to comply with the demand of the plaintiff to implement the agreement for sale, the plaintiff was obliged to institute other Suit No. 9 of 1959 against defendant Nos 1 to 3 for specific performance of contract and for setting aside pasta and kabala executed in favour of defendant Nos. 2 and 3 also for confirmation of plaintiff's possession in the disputed land. The plaintiff obtained a decree for specific performance of contract against the defendant No. 1 but his prayers for setting aside the patta executed by defendant No. 1 in favour of defendant Nos. 2 and 3 and also for confirmation of possession in the suit land were refused on the ground that it was beyond the scope of the suit. The plaintiff got the kabala in respect of the disputed land erected and registered through the Court but in the meantime defendant Nos 2 and 3 managed to dispossess the plaintiff from the disputed land and erected certain structures thereon. The plaintiff has therefore been compelled to institute this suit. 

 3. Defendant No. 1 did not appear in the suit but it was contested by defendant Nos. 2 and 3 who filed a joint written statement contenting, inter alia, that the suit was barred by limitation and was not maintainable in the present form and that it was defendant No.1 who had set up the plaintiff to prosecute the suit on his behalf. The substantive defence case is that defendant Nos. 2 and 3 were tenants in respect of the disputed land under one Indra Narayan Datta in 1917 Defendant No. 1 after having acquired the interest of the said Indra Narayan recognized defendant Nos. 2 and 3 as tenants of the disputed land. Thereafter, in 1949 defendant No. 1 contracted to sell the land to defendant Nos. 2 and 3 for and of Rs. 10,000/- out of which Rs. 2,000/- was paid but due to laches on the part of defendant No. 1, there was delay in execution of the promised deed. Thereafter, when in 1957 defendant Nos. 2 and 3 passed upon defendant No. 1 for implementation of the contract in their favour, defendant No. 1 executed a patta for a term of 9 years in favour of defendant Nos. 2 and 3 on 15-4-57 and also a kabala in respect of the rent-receiving interest of the said land in favour of the wives of the said defendants on 15-4-57 and received the balance of consideration money. But defendant No 1 having entered into an unholy alliance with the plaintiff executed a collusive bainanama in his favour and did not register the aforesaid although the patta was duly registered on 15-4-57. In consequence, defendant Nos. 2 and 3 were obliged to institute the other Suit No. 23 of 1957 against defendant No. 1 and others for registration of the said kabala. The contesting defendants have been in possession of the disputed land and have constructed huts and building on the said land alter raising its level or business purpose to the knowledge of both the plaintiff and defendant No. 1 without any obstruction from any of them and as such the plaintiff has no right, title and interest in the said land. 

 4. Upon the aforesaid pleadings certain issues were framed and evidence was led by the parties in respect of their respective contentions. The High court on a consideration of the facts and circumstances of the case and evidence on record came to the finding that defendant Nos. 2 and 3 had been possessing the disputed land since 1946 as tenants and thereafter as purchasers on the basis of purchase from defendant No. 1 in 1949 and that they been possessing the disputed land since 1949 by virtue of the right acquired by them by making improvements of, and construction on the suit land. The learned Subordinate Judge however held that defendant No. 1 had contracted to sell and thereafter sold the land in 1949 to the defendant Nos. 2 and 1 for valuable consideration. On the question whether the patta marked Ext. C. executed by defendant No. 1 in favour of defendant Nos 2 and 3 and the kabala marked Ext. D executed by defendant No.1 in favour of the wives of defendant Nos. 2 and 3 constituted a single transaction amounting to a sale of he disputed land, was placed on of the contesting defendants in the trial court upon the decision reported in Md. Hossain Mia Vs. Member, Board of Revenue, 14 D.L R Dacca. page 87 in which it was held that a deed of lease followed immediately by a deed of sale of the rent-receiving interest of the lease hold property in favour of the same person constituted a transaction of out and our sale of the property But the learned Subordinate Judge appears to have distinguished the said case on the ground that in the instant case the kabala Ext. D was not in favour of defendant Nos. 2 and 3, the repents of the Patta, Ext. C but in favour of their and as such was of the opinion that the deed of lease, Ext. C and the kabala, Ext. D did not constitute a single transaction of sale, but were two separate transaction. On that view of the matter the deed of lease, Ext C executed by defendant No 1 in favour of defendant Nos. 2 and 3 was held to have been hit by section 9 and section 75A of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, and as such was null and void in the eye of law The learned Subordinate Judge however, held that defendant Nos. 2 and 3 acquired good title to the disputed land on the basis of continuous possession of the same for more than 12 years. He came to further findings that defendant No. 1 was in charge of the prosecution of the suit on behalf of the plaintiff and that the bainanama, Ext. 1 purported to be executed by defendant No. 1 in favour of the plaintiff was a collusive document, the suit was dismissed on the basis of the aforesaid findings. 

 10. Mr. Mozammel Huq, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the appellant contends that both the learned Subordinate Judge and the learned Additional District Judge were wrong in taking the view that the patta. Ext. C and the kabala, Ext. D in respect of the rent receiving interest arising in consequence of patta, Ext. C being not in favour of the same person, one is being in favour of defendant Nos. 2 and 3 and the other being in favour of their wives cannot be construed as par and parcel of the one and same transaction. According to the learned Advocate the wives were merely benamdars of their husbands and as a matter of fact both the documents constitute one and same transaction. In support of his contention, he has relied upon the decision of the Supreme Court of Pakistan in Manir Ahmed Vs.
